title: Where Her Story Is Told
hookLine: the goddess makes her last promises, and night one of Navaratri gives her a seat
carry: she stays where her story is told

cards: The last battle of the Devi Mahatmya is over. Shumbha, the demon king who took the gods' heaven, is dead, the world grows calm, and the gods sing to the goddess one more time. Then she answers them.
With promises about the future: about anyone, anywhere, who will someday tell this story. Tonight, night one of Navaratri, is where those promises come home.

teach.b: You met Navaratri on day eighty; tonight, how it opens. In the twelfth chapter the goddess makes her promises, in paraphrase. Whoever praises me with these hymns, I will take away their troubles.
Where this story is recited in my shrine, I will never leave; my presence stays there. Whatever worship is offered me, by someone who knows the rules or someone who doesn't, I accept with love.
And at the great worship held every autumn, whoever hears my story with devotion will be freed from troubles. Then she vanishes. Two of those promises explain how Navaratri begins.

teach.h: WHERE MY STORY IS TOLD, I STAY.
teach.b: The first: her presence stays where her story is told.

teach.h: NIGHT ONE: A POT, A COCONUT, A SEAT.
teach.b: So on night one, in many homes, she's given a seat. A pot of water, the kalash, is set out with mango leaves and a coconut at its mouth, and with prayer the goddess is invited to dwell in it for the nine nights.

In some homes in North India, barley is sown in soil beside it, and by the end the dish is green. Some families read her story across the nights. Either way, for nine nights the house becomes her shrine.
The second promise is the one to hold onto if you've ever worried you're doing it wrong.

teach.h: KNOWN OR NOT KNOWN, I ACCEPT IT.
teach.b: Known or not known, she says, I accept it with love. Plenty of families today don't remember every step their grandparents knew. Many teachers read this verse as her answer: she looks at the devotion, not the checklist.

teach.h: GIVE HER A SEAT. SHE STAYS.
teach.b: Give her a seat, and she stays.

how: In many homes the first day of Navaratri begins with ghatasthapana: a water pot (kalash) with mango leaves and a coconut is installed, and the goddess is invited to dwell in it for the nine nights; in parts of North India barley is sown beside it to sprout. Elsewhere the first night opens with a lamp, dance, a display of dolls, or recitation of the Devi Mahatmya.

games.q: what does “navaratri as a nine-night curriculum” mean?
o: nine nights of feasting with no goddess behind them
a single night of dancing that ends the harvest season
nine nights with the goddess given a seat in the home

p: a water pot where she is invited to stay

s: in the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess promises to stay where her story is recited
where it's recited in her shrine, she says, she'll never leave.
she accepts worship only when every rule is followed
known or not known, she says, she accepts it with love.
the barley sown on night one is meant to sprout that same night
it's tended across the nights; the shoots come by the end.

games.q: it's night one. you're setting up the kalash for the first time, from a video, and you're not sure you've done it right. what does the goddess say in her own book?
o: only perfect worship counts, so start over.
known or not known, I accept it with love.
wait until a priest can do it for you.
games.why: in chapter twelve she promises to accept worship offered knowingly or unknowingly, with love, and to stay where her story is told.

practice: If you keep a shrine, or even a shelf, light a lamp or a candle tonight and invite the goddess in your own words, the way families do on night one: come, Ma, stay with us these nine nights.
Don't worry about saying it right; she said she'd take it with love either way. Then sit for a few breaths with the flame, as if a guest has just arrived.
If you don't pray, sit with the light anyway, and notice what it's like to make room in a home for something you can't see.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights for the goddess, opened by giving her a seat, because she promised to stay where her story is told.

orig.note: Sanskrit kalaśa: a water pot. on night one of Navaratri the goddess is invited to dwell in it.

carryVoice: Your line: she stays where her story is told. Night one gives her a seat. Night one, done.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya 12 (the goddess's promises: her presence where the story is recited; worship known or unknown accepted with love; the great autumn worship)
Ghatasthapana: installing the kalash and sowing barley on Navaratri's first day
